title: Levirate Marriage
lead: The custom that when a man died without a son, his brother married the widow, and their first son carried on the dead man's name and inheritance (Deuteronomy 25:5–10). It lies behind the stories of Tamar (Genesis 38) and Ruth, and behind the Sadducees' question to Jesus (Matthew 22:23–33).

sections.h: The custom in the Law and the Gospels
sections.b: Deuteronomy 25:5–10 lays down the duty: a brother who lives with the family marries his dead brother's childless widow, and the first son carries the dead man's name, "so that his name will not be blotted out of Israel." A brother who refuses is shamed at the gate: the widow pulls off his sandal and spits in his face. Genesis 38 shows the custom before the Law, and the Sadducees use it to mock the resurrection (Matthew 22:23–33). Later Jewish law, in the Mishnah tractate Yevamot, came to prefer the release ceremony (halitzah) over the marriage itself.
